proposed_edges.relationship: Wolfe adapts Mauss’s total social phenomenon to analyse anthropology as a total discursive practice participating in colonial settlement.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 1999 introduction 3 explicitly identifies the adaptation, while note 6 quotes Mauss 1925 [1970]:1 on simultaneously religious, legal, moral, economic, aesthetic and morphological institutions. Wolfe treats anthropological debates as primary data rather than adjudicating their claims about Indigenous life. This is a particular methodological resource, not equivalence between the two complete projects or a newly read Mauss original; bracketed 1970 does not become first publication.

proposed_edges.relationship: Wolfe uses Spivak’s distinction between exposing mechanisms and making individuals speak to explain his refusal of ethnographic ventriloquism.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own introduction 4 invokes Spivak 1988:288 while distinguishing the analysis of anthropological constructions from an attempt to recuperate an allegedly pristine Indigenous voice behind them. Political and empirical methodological limits converge in his argument. This records his explicit use of a particular distinction, not proof he adopted all of Spivak’s work, a claim Indigenous people had no voice, or a newly read Spivak original; the cited original title is not guessed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Chakrabarty supervised and commented on the entire doctoral draft from which substantial portions of Wolfe’s first book developed.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own acknowledgments vii distinguish three successive supervisors, Maurice Bloch, Greg Dening and finally Chakrabarty; the last read and commented on the whole draft. This is specific critical scholarly input to the thesis, not a claim he alone formed Wolfe or read the final 1999 book. Wolfe explicitly separates the later rewritten book and the whole-book readings by Phillip Darby and Michele Grossman. No particular adopted revision or common theoretical doctrine is invented.

proposed_edges.relationship: Wong traces his comparative historical social science and the initial framing of China Transformed to his training with Charles Tilly.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own original 2017 Fudan interview, first and fourth answers, explicitly identifies Tilly’s historical social science as the work he wanted to do and his undergraduate training as the immediate reason for the Europe–China comparison. This is Wong’s retrospective statement of specific intellectual formation, not an inference from a shared university, an independently audited annual meeting chronology, or proof he adopted all of Tilly’s models. The displayed English answers ground the claim; the accompanying Chinese rendering is not treated as a separate interview or expanded quotation.

proposed_edges.relationship: Wong takes Braudel’s relational regional analysis as a resource for comparing Asian histories beyond national and Eurocentric frames.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2001 article, translated into French by Pierre-Étienne Will, 5–9, especially 6 and 8–9, presents the Mediterranean as a framework between nation and globe and emphasizes changing human connections rather than fixed cultural boundaries. Wong distinguishes Braudel’s flexible, contingent regions from Skinner’s more enduring hierarchical macroregions while examining how Asian histories can use the approach. This is a particular analytic resource, not evidence that every Asian region is a Mediterranean replica or a newly read Braudel original. Note 1 specifies use of the 1966 edition; note 2 separately cites a 1976 manifestation. The publisher’s 2017 online migration date does not replace the original February 2001 issue date.

proposed_edges.relationship: Higginbotham uses Barthes’s account of myth and metalanguage to explain race’s power to organize and obscure other social relations.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 1992:254–255/notes 10–11 quotes Mythologies and uses its conceptual vocabulary to explain race as an ideological fact with real effects, neither natural biological essence nor a harmless illusion. Her specific race/gender/class argument remains her own adaptation. The cited Annette Lavers translation (1972), pages 114–115,118,120, was not independently read, and no first-publication claim is inferred from that translation date.

proposed_edges.relationship: Higginbotham uses Althusser’s ideological state apparatuses to explain institutions’ production of racialized gender and class meanings.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 254/note 9 names schools, family, welfare agencies, hospitals and media while explaining how socially constructed gender and class acquire racialized normative meanings. This particular explanatory use coexists with separately credited Foucault, not exclusive derivation or blanket Althusserian affiliation. The cited Ben Brewster translation in Lenin and Philosophy (1972),165 is not newly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Higginbotham uses Du Bois’s account of divided subjectivity when explaining race as both imposed classification and a language of collective resistance.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 267/note 47 explicitly invokes Du Bois’s 1903 two-ness alongside the collective nation-within-a-nation formulation, retaining Martin Delany’s separate credit. Earlier 252/note 3 also locates anti-biological racial analysis in Du Bois’s work. This is specific conceptual/historical use, not a claim she uncritically adopted every Du Bois racial formulation. Her separate discussion of the 1897 Conservation of Races remains qualified. The cited Souls manifestation is 1970; the original is not newly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Higginbotham places Du Bois’s 1897 racial-spiritual uniqueness within her critical account of romantic racialism and essentialized Black national culture.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 269/note 55, continuing 270, identifies Conservation of Races as an example of the spiritual special-gift conception, then distinguishes the liberating intent of cultural self-recovery from its obscuring of Black heterogeneity. Her critical analytic target is the specific 1897 formulation and a broader racial-national tradition, not all of Du Bois’s changing work or a denial of its anti-racist aims. Fredrickson’s romantic-racialism terminology and Appiah’s separately cited criticism retain credit; original Du Bois/Appiah works unread. Her positive double-consciousness resource remains separate.

proposed_edges.relationship: Higginbotham uses Anderson’s imagined-community framework to situate racialized national belonging as constructed rather than natural.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 268–269/note 52 moves from the forging of a common African diasporic ancestry to non-unique national imaginings and explicitly cites Anderson’s limited, sovereign community. This bounded supporting resource is not proof Anderson originated all Black nationalist thought or that she endorsed biological racial nationalism. The original 1983 book,14–16, remains unread; the cited edition is not replaced with a later revision.

proposed_edges.relationship: Higginbotham uses Williams’s account of language as continual creation to support her analysis of racial language appropriated for resistance.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 270/note 57 cites Marxism and Literature,31, at the point where she explains Black appropriation of productive linguistic power. Bakhtin’s double-voiced discourse and Fanon’s cultural self-recovery retain their separate roles. This particular conceptual support does not establish complete adoption of cultural materialism; original 1977 book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Higginbotham uses Cott’s history of passionlessness as a specific counterpoint when distinguishing racialized representations of women’s sexuality.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 263/note 33 names Cott’s analysis of evangelical Protestantism and later science in producing passionlessness for northern white women. The main paragraph contrasts changing white sexual ideals with persistent racist sexualization of Black women, alongside separately credited Laqueur, Jordan and Gilman. This is a bounded historiographic resource, not a claim Cott’s entire work ignored race or a new personal formative influence. Original Cott essay unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Higginbotham values Kelley’s analysis of violence and imprisonment as a resource for showing how her metalanguage framework illuminates the carceral turn in Black women’s history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2017:635 explicitly calls Kelley’s historiographic discussion particularly valuable for that specific task, following the introduction’s description at 628–629. This is scholarly uptake in her later forum response, not a causal source of her 1992 article. LeFlouria, Muhammad and the other historians she discusses retain separate credit. Kelley’s complete original forum essay is not newly read. Her bibliography prints a discrepant 509–600; publisher metadata verifies the original article as Signs 42:3,590–600, DOI 10.1086/689623, without silently treating the printed typo as the correct range.

proposed_edges.relationship: Kealey adopts Thompson’s focus on class as developing behavior and defends the materiality of culture while requiring that British insights be tested in Canada.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 1981: 85–87 explicitly stands with Thompson and Raymond Williams on culture, then distinguishes objective class parameters from Thompson’s terrain of changing behavior and class-for-itself. He concedes some cultural work neglects economy and that imported methods require contextual demonstration. This is his specific methodological resource, beyond the existing broader field route 890, not wholesale agreement or a fresh reading of the complete Thompson originals. Williams and Hobsbawm retain distinct roles.

proposed_edges.relationship: Kealey uses Raymond Williams’s account of culture and revisable hegemony to explain both working-class resistance and its limits.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 1981: 80/n 30–31 uses Keywords and Politics and Letters to frame culture as activity and a whole way of life; 85/n 42 defends its materiality. At 89/n 59 and 90/n 61, Williams supplies the distinctions between class conflict and class struggle and the account of continuously renewed, resisted hegemony. Gramsci is explicitly mediated through Williams, and separate Eley–Nield discussion is credited. Culture does not require universal solidarity or perpetual militancy; defeat needs explanation. These are Raymond’s works, not Eric Williams or every cited Williams; originals unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Kealey uses Hobsbawm’s account of artisans’ respectability and class consciousness when interpreting skilled Canadian workers’ institutions and politics.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 1981: 85/n 45 invokes Hobsbawm on the objective side of class. At 87/n 50 he uses The Aristocracy of Labour Reconsidered to reject the equation of respectability with simple embourgeoisement, then connects the findings to Hamilton and Toronto research 87–88. The labour-aristocracy literature is plural and contested; the cited Canadian studies and worker agency retain distinct credit. This is specific use, not proof that every British model fits Canada or a fresh reading of the cited originals.

proposed_edges.relationship: Kealey invokes Tilly’s aspiration to overcome disciplinary division between history and sociology as a stated aim of his edited collection.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 1988 introduction 5 explicitly quotes Tilly’s 1981 aspiration and presents the volume as pursuing it. His opening 1 describes the editorial project, and 5 insists on empirical research while acknowledging methodological differences. This is a particular editorial and methodological resource, not formal supervision, adoption of all Tilly’s collective-action models, or credit for every contributor’s article. Tilly and Michael Katz’s shared quantitative-project role on 4 remains distinct; original Tilly book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Kealey explicitly says that confronting McKay’s materialist critique of Thompson and culturalism benefited his thinking.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 1981: 91/n 63 calls the unpublished 1980 Towards a Materialist Approach to Canadian Labour History a particularly substantive critique and explicitly acknowledges benefit from confronting it. This is direct Kealey testimony about the critical resource; the unpublished text itself is unread. It is distinct from the later published 1981–82 Historians, Anthropology, and the Concept of Culture, whose complete original remains unread this turn; neither agreement with every objection nor identity of versions is assumed. McKay also receives draft-comment credit 94.

proposed_edges.relationship: Kealey uses Stedman Jones’s discussion of history and the social sciences to insist on critical, historically informed borrowing of methods.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 1981: 86/n 46 calls From Historical Sociology to Theoretical History the best discussion he knows of the problem of borrowing concepts without understanding disciplinary debates. The same note calls Class Expression Versus Social Control a specific critique of unreflective borrowing; 91/n 64 returns to the former. Thompson and the opposed defense of social control by Moorhouse retain distinct credit. This is a particular methodological resource, not agreement with Stedman Jones’s later language-of-class arguments or a new reading of those original articles.

proposed_edges.relationship: Kealey calls Cook’s worry that a golden age of Canadian historical writing was ending premature, arguing that working-class studies could transform the historical synthesis.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 1978: 116/n 1–2 identifies Cook’s limited-identities call and Golden Age essay. At 135 he calls the earlier pluralism refreshing and liberating while disputing analytical separation of class, ethnicity and place, then explicitly labels Cook’s pessimistic forecast premature. The criticism retains the acknowledged achievement and does not undo Cook’s distinct teaching influence 2694 or claim all Cook scholarship rejects labour history. Original Cook 1967/1977 texts not newly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Kealey criticizes Berger’s handling of the new history for confusing critical inquiry with a mission to provide a positive national account.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 1988 introduction 2 quotes Berger’s 1986 conclusion 320 and immediately charges confusion between critical scholarship and national mythology. He introduces Berger as even-handed before criticizing this aspect, then compares Careless’s changing position 2–3, already 998. This records Kealey’s reading of the quoted passage, not an independently established summary of the entire unread Berger book. The later 1995 quoted acknowledgment of finding little to contest in Berger’s labour-history summary, already group 941, is preserved.

new_sources.title: R. Bin Wong, interview on research in Chinese economic history, Fudan School of Economics, 2017
new_sources.citation: R. Bin Wong, interview conducted and compiled by Lu Guanwen (陆冠文), Fudan University School of Economics, 19 May 2017; bilingual English answers and Chinese rendering.

verification.note: Complete original university interview read: six questions and answers, both language presentations, interviewer credit and dated introduction. Tilly’s specific comparative social-science formation is his own first/fourth-answer account. His Japanese scholarly training is important but no Japanese individual is named. Fairbank in the third answer concerns the field’s development, not by itself a personal influence confession; editorial biographical teacher labels are not automatically intellectual debt. English answers provide the proposal, and no divergence between the two languages is silently merged.

new_sources.title: R. Bin Wong, “Entre monde et nation: les régions braudéliennes en Asie,” 2001
new_sources.citation: R. Bin Wong, “Entre monde et nation: les régions braudéliennes en Asie,” translated by Pierre-Étienne Will, Annales. Histoire, Sciences Sociales 56, no. 1 (January–February 2001): 5–41.

verification.note: Actual original journal opening 5–9, with all notes 1–4, read through official Persée archive page/text endpoints; original first page and all four subsequent text pages retained. Complete article not claimed. Publisher French and English abstracts and notes 1–3 independently checked for date, Braudel manifestation and Skinner identity; February 2001 issue distinct from May 2017 online publication. Translator Pierre-Étienne Will receives explicit credit, not mistaken joint authorship. Braudel’s original and Skinner’s original writings unread; later maritime examples and regional-state analysis beyond 9 unread.

cpl129_wolfe_1999_intro.note: Fresh licensed publisher preview of the original 1999 Cassell edition read: complete acknowledgments vii, credits viii, terminology ix, complete Introduction 1–7 and all notes 1–9; title, imprint and contents checked. Opening chapter 1 at 9 and first two paragraphs of 10 incidentally read, not the complete chapter. Mauss adaptation 3/note 6, Spivak anti-ventriloquism distinction 4, and Chakrabarty’s complete doctoral-draft input vii checked. Doctoral draft is distinct from the rewritten final book, and all three supervisors retain credit. Stronger Stocking example, Dening/Bloch supervision, Asad, Rose, LaCapra and other particular resources or critiques remain explicit missing-endpoint holds. Original Mauss/Spivak and other cited works, complete later chapters and complete monographs remain unread. This expands the earlier 1–2 reading without rewriting its historical qualification.

higginbotham_race.note: Fresh complete original Signs 17:2 (1992),251–274 and all 68 notes read from institutional single-article teaching share; course syllabus explicitly assigns this essay alongside the 2017 retrospective. Actual PDF pages for 254–255,263,269–270 visually compared with extracted text, whose right-margin OCR sometimes drops letters. Barthes’s myth/metalanguage, Althusser’s institutional apparatuses, Du Bois’s two-ness and particular 1897 romantic-racialism limit, Anderson’s imagined national belonging, Williams’s regenerative language and Cott’s passionlessness counterpoint checked in actual body and notes. Earlier Hine feedback/dissemblance and Foucault/James C. Scott resources preserved, not duplicated. Stronger missing Bakhtin, Fields (both resource and criticism), Carby, Collins criticism, Cooper and E. Frances White remain explicit. All cited theoretical/historical originals unread; the 1992 in-press Righteous Discontent note is not treated as verified actual publication date or full book reading.

js_reception_higginbotham_2017.note: Fresh complete own Signs 42:3 (2017),628–642, all 12 notes and references read from institutional single-article teaching share; preceding article bibliography at the top of 628 belongs to another contributor and is excluded. Actual 635 visually collated for Kelley’s particular carceral historiography resource. Dates and scope corroborated against original publisher DOI 10.1086/689893. This retrospective explicitly credits equally the Black women historians Hine, Elsa Barkley Brown, Painter and Hunter, not European theory alone. Strong missing contemporary methodological resources, forthcoming Owens supervision, liberation/pleasure and costs of respectability retain their own limits. The full original forum essays, monographs and dissertation remain unread. Prior Joan Scott criticism stays exact; cited Said/James Scott are resources for Camp, not automatically her own personal formation.

wcreq_kealey_1981.note: Fresh actual original 1981 journal article retrieved through its authorized Érudit preservation copy, 29 leaves including wrapper, and independently rendered through original LLT PDF. Selected 67–69 and 80–94 with associated notes read; 85 and 91 visually checked. Original March 1980 conference delivery and 1981 publication distinguished; this is not a reply composed after the companion Bercuson essay. Exact note 45 (Hobsbawm), 42 (Williams), 46 (Stedman Jones), 61 (hegemony through Williams) and 63 (unpublished McKay) visually or textually collated, avoiding OCR numbering errors. Collective Hann/Kealey/Linda Kealey/Warrian and Palmer credits, strong missing Gutman/Montgomery, cultural limits, critical positions and acknowledgments retained. Other 70–79 and complete cited books/articles unread.

pe138_kealey_acadiensis_1978.note: Fresh actual original UNB journal PDF retrieved, selected 116–117 and 134–135 with notes read; 135 visually checked. Cook limited-identities and Golden Age references kept distinct, including the source’s displayed 1967 journal-volume anomaly rather than silently correcting it. Specific forecast criticism retains refreshing and liberating pluralism and the need to incorporate ethnicity/place. Gender/family and municipal-politics research priorities 134 remain. Other article pages and original cited works unread.

pe138_kealey_cgr_1988.note: Fresh actual AU Press-hosted CCLH 1988 reprint PDF through successful original publisher web rendering, complete introduction 1–5 and references 5–7 read; direct network 406 is not a body. Copyright 1988 and original CJS special-issue/reprint status distinguished from 1985 invitation and 1986 submissions. Tilly editorial aspiration, Berger specific quotation/criticism, Skocpol categorical test with retained praise, Bradbury family-economy resources and collective article authors preserved. Later chapters are separately authored and not assigned to Kealey; only the introduction is read, not the whole 178-leaf collection.
